name: Saint-Germain-des-Pres
short_description: Oldest church in Paris with origins in the 6th century, anchor of the Left Bank literary and existentialist neighbourhood

beats.script_body: You are standing before the oldest church in Paris, built between 990 and 1014 AD in the Romanesque style. Look carefully at the second chancel — those small columns are survivors from the original 6th-century basilica that honoured Saint Vincent, before Saint Germain took over as patron. In 1163, a larger choir was built to accommodate growing numbers of monks, along with a bell-tower and majestic portal. Pope Alexander III himself presided over the ceremony — and just weeks later, he would lay the cornerstone of Notre-Dame cathedral across the river.
physical_cues: small columns in second chancel from 6th-century basilica
beats.source_passage: the oldest church in Paris. It even retains some small columns from the first 6th-century basilica

beats.script_body: On 2 September 1792, the abbey prison that once stood across Boulevard Saint-Germain became the site of one of the Revolution's bloodiest episodes. Rumours of a plot against 'the good people' of Paris were deliberately spread, bells were rung, pamphlets distributed. After a mock trial, 100 prisoners including many priests were executed on the first day. By the third day, hundreds of people had been killed at or near the junction of rue Bonaparte and rue de l'Abbaye, their bodies piled in the abbey gardens. The killers worked by torchlight through the night, then tried to erase all evidence, ordering prison concierges to wash away blood with water and vinegar.
physical_cues: junction of rue Bonaparte and rue de l'Abbaye
beats.source_passage: the bloody massacres of 2, 3 and 4 September 1792 were triggered

beats.script_body: The abbey of Saint-Germain was once a city within a city, home to about 10,000 people, its domains reaching into today's 15th arrondissement. It answered directly to the Pope, ensuring political independence. Its 13th-century chapel, designed by Pierre de Montreuil — the same architect behind Sainte-Chapelle — was destroyed during the Revolution. When 15,000 tons of gunpowder stored in the dining hall ignited alongside a huge stock of coal, the explosion and fire devoured nearly everything, including a library of 50,000 volumes. Yet miraculously, most of its 7,000 manuscripts survived, including Pascal's original Pensées.
physical_cues: little garden before the church on site of cloister
vestiges of medieval chapel arcades in garden
beats.source_passage: about 10,000 people were living around the abbey, a city within a city

beats.script_body: On the eastern wall of the church, look for the spectacular enamelled sandstone portico affixed to the garden of Square Felix Desruelles. It was manufactured by the celebrated Sevres workshops for the 1900 Universal Exposition. During the Revolution, the church was used as a refinery for saltpetre, leaving it in sorry state. Victor Baltard undertook its restoration, while Hippolyte Flandrin contributed the murals you can see inside.
physical_cues: enamelled sandstone portico on eastern wall
beats.source_passage: A spectacular enamelled sandstone portico is affixed to its eastern wall, manufactured by the celebrated Sevres workshops for the 1900 Universal Exposition

opening_hours_basis: Door; hours are the place's own OpenStreetMap tag: Mo,Su 09:30-20:00; Tu-Fr 07:30-20:00; Sa 08:30-20:00.
visit_basis: Oldest church in Paris with a Romanesque tower and painted medieval nave; interior takes about 20 min, exterior square and cafe corner a few minutes more.
judgement_basis: A working church where silence is expected and running is impossible, with no free quiet seating suited to talk (the small adjacent square sits beside busy boulevard traffic), but the busy lit Left Bank crossroads outside is well-peopled after dark.
queue_basis: An active parish church with an open door and free entry that visitors walk straight into, so there is no ticket desk or security to stand in.

name: Place de Furstemberg
short_description: One of the most charming small squares in Paris on the site of the former abbey palace courtyard, and home to the Musée Delacroix in the painter's last studio at no. 6.

beats.script_body: In January 1857, Delacroix was living in the artists' quarter of La Nouvelle-Athenes when he was finally elected to the Academie des Beaux-Arts — after seven rejections. Seriously ill with laryngitis, he needed to be closer to his murals at Saint-Sulpice. He found this apartment through his dealer Haro, though converting it into a studio was, as he wrote in his journal, 'the devil's own job.' His fierce Breton housekeeper Jenny Le Guillou moved with him and increasingly barred visitors, especially women. He died here in 1863 at the age of 65. On his first morning, he wrote: 'I awoke to find the sun shining in the most welcoming way on the houses opposite my window.'
physical_cues: courtyard with arched entrance and uneven cobblestones
beats.source_passage: the Musee (or atelier) Delacroix, located in the last home of the painter, where he died in 1863

beats.script_body: Over fifty years after Delacroix's death, in 1929, prominent artists including Bonnard and Signac founded La Societe des amis de Delacroix to preserve his memory. They rented these dilapidated premises, had them restored, and began organizing temporary exhibitions. By 1963, the Society persuaded the State to purchase the premises and establish a permanent museum. Today the collection charts Delacroix's artistic development through drawings, sketches, studies, and personal documents.
physical_cues: museum interior with drawings and sketches
beats.source_passage: in 1929, some prominent artists, Bonnard and Signac among them, founded a society to promote the memory of Delacroix

beats.script_body: This bewitching square is named after Abbot Egon de Furstemberg, who in 1691 reconstructed the abbey's brick-and-stone Renaissance palace. You are standing on the site of the palace's main courtyard, turned into a square in the 18th century. The bright pink house at numbers 6 and 8 was painted to look like brick — because real brick was very expensive — and served as stables and carriage sheds for the palace. Henry Miller described it differently: 'A deserted spot, bleak, spectral at night, containing in the centre four black trees; these four bare trees have the poetry of T.S. Eliot.'
beats.source_passage: named after Egon de Furstemberg, the abbot who in 1691 reconstructed the abbey's brick-and-stone Renaissance palace

opening_hours_basis: An open public square whose whole value stands in the open on the pavement, not gated.
visit_basis: Small enclosed square with a central lamppost and paulownia trees to stand in and circle; the Musée Delacroix at no. 6 is a compact studio-and-apartment museum with a small garden, roughly 20-25 min inside.
judgement_basis: A small quiet paved square set off the road with low kerbs and no full enclosure or gates, so a child could wander into the adjoining lane; it has benches and low walls around the central paulownia trees quiet enough to talk, and being an open, lit through-square it stays accessible after dark.
queue_basis: An open public square with no door and no gate; the Musée Delacroix on it has its own small desk, but the square itself is walked into freely with no line.

name: L'Hotel Paris
short_description: Luxury hotel at 13 rue des Beaux-Arts where Oscar Wilde died on 30 November 1900, when it was the run-down Hotel d'Alsace.

beats.script_body: At number 13 rue des Beaux-Arts stands L'Hotel, now a luxury establishment but in 1900 a run-down place with appalling plumbing called Hotel Alsace. It was here that Oscar Wilde, poverty-stricken and exiled from Britain, lived 'beyond his means' as he famously put it, and died on 30 November 1900. His room has been recreated and constitutes a second Parisian shrine for the brilliant exile. His grave lies in Pere-Lachaise cemetery across the city.
physical_cues: hotel facade at 13 rue des Beaux-Arts
beats.source_passage: In 1900, when poverty-stricken Oscar Wilde stayed here, it was a run-down, cheap place with appalling plumbing, called Hotel Alsace

opening_hours_basis: A working luxury hotel viewed and passed as a facade on the street; not a gated visitor attraction.
visit_basis: A working luxury hotel facade viewed from the narrow street where Oscar Wilde died; a few minutes to read the plaque and look up, nothing publicly enterable as a visit.
judgement_basis: This is a private luxury hotel frontage on a narrow street: no traffic-free run for children, no free public seating on the pavement, but the doorway sits on a lit, populated central street so a person left standing outside would be fine at night.
queue_basis: A working luxury hotel viewed from the street on a walking tour; there is no public ticketed entry and no queue to stand in outside.

name: Rue Visconti
short_description: Narrow historic alley in the 6th arrondissement, once called 'Little Geneva' as a Huguenot refuge, home to Racine, Balzac, Delacroix, and Adrienne Lecouvreur.

beats.script_body: This narrow alley opened in the 16th century and, being in a remote and therefore safer area, became home to Paris's Huguenot community, earning the nickname 'Little Geneva.' In 1559, the first synod of the French Reformed Church was held here, attended by delegates of 72 churches. When the Huguenots convened again months later, police surprised them, but all except four managed to escape. Among these Protestant residents was architect Jean-Baptiste Androuet du Cerceau, builder of the Pont-Neuf and friend of Henri IV, who preferred 'to part with the friendship of the King, than to go to mass.'
physical_cues: early period houses at n 5, 7 and 9
beats.source_passage: situated in what was then a remote and therefore safer area, became the home of the Huguenots, and dubbed 'Little Geneva'

beats.script_body: At number 16 lived Adrienne Lecouvreur, one of the most idolized actresses of the Comedie-Francaise in the early 18th century. Among her famous lovers was Marechal Maurice de Saxe, hero of the battle of Fontenoy and great-grandfather of George Sand. Voltaire was among her close friends and was by her side on 20 March 1730 when she died. No one knew the exact cause — some said it was for love of the Marechal, others that she was poisoned by a rival.
beats.source_passage: Adrienne Lecouvreur, a much idolized actresses of the Comedie-Francaise, who lived at n 16 in the early 18th century

beats.script_body: At numbers 17-19, Balzac lived in 1826-1828 during the early days of his career, trying his hand at business ventures. He opened a printing house here which brought in no money, and handed it over to the son of his much older friend and mentor Madame de Berny, in whose hands the business fared much better. It was probably here that Stendhal's masterpiece Le Rouge et le Noir was first printed. Later, Delacroix painted some of his greatest works in this same building, including L'Entree des Croises a Constantinople.
beats.source_passage: at n 17/19 across the street, Balzac lived in the early days of his career

beats.script_body: At number 24, the great playwright Racine spent the last seven years of his life. He settled here at the age of 53 in poor health and out of favour with Louis XIV, partly because the King had lost interest in theatre and partly because Racine was a Jansenist at a time when they were outlawed. Unlike his rival Corneille who died in destitution, Racine had a spacious apartment, 14 servants, a carriage, two horses and a small post-chaise. Both he and his wife were devoted Christians; of their seven children, four intended to become nuns.
beats.source_passage: Racine spent the last seven years of his life at n 24

beats.script_body: A plaque at 26 rue de Seine says the writer Saint-Amant died here on 29 December 1661. But the plaque barely hints at the true story. Saint-Amant died not in his bed but in the cabaret Le Petit-Maure on this site, and it was not a natural death. He was a highly-regarded writer and one of the first Academicians, but when he rashly targeted the great Conde in a satirical verse, the prince had him dragged to the Pont-Neuf and thrashed vigorously, then dragged back to the cabaret, where he was dumped and left to die two days later, aged 67.
physical_cues: plaque at n 26 rue de Seine on corner of rue Visconti
beats.source_passage: a plaque at n 26 rue de Seine, on the corner house of rue Visconti, says that the writer Saint-Amant died here on 29 December 1621

beats.script_body: At number 31 rue de Seine, Aurore Dupin first settled on her own, aged 27, after separating from her husband. To assert herself, she sported men's clothes and adopted the pen-name George Sand, with a deliberately British spelling. A century later, in 1920, Raymond Duncan — brother of dancer Isadora Duncan — set up his academy at this same address, dedicated to reviving Ancient Greek culture. He taught Greek arts and crafts including weaving and sandal-making, and went around in a Greek-style robe and sandals with a wreath of leaves on his head.
physical_cues: understated elegant facade at n 31 with lovely courtyard
beats.source_passage: at n 31, an understated, elegant facade conceals a lovely courtyard. This was where Aurore Dupin first settled on her own

opening_hours_basis: A public street open to the air at all times, not gated.
visit_basis: Narrow historic alley you walk end to end reading plaques for Racine, Balzac and Delacroix; the value is entirely along its length, nothing to enter.
judgement_basis: A narrow historic alley with no pavement separation and no public seating, echoing and deserted at night with no through-lighting or crowds, so it fails all three tests.
queue_basis: A narrow open alley you walk down; it has no door, no ticket, and no line.

name: Ecole des Beaux-Arts
short_description: France's preeminent fine arts school at 14 rue Bonaparte, occupying the former convent of the Petits-Augustins built on Queen Margot's estate in 1608.

beats.script_body: The Beaux-Arts school at 14 rue Bonaparte occupies part of a convent built by Marguerite de Valois in 1608 on her estate. Devoutly religious, she had vowed to erect a temple to the Patriarch Jacob. She added La Chapelle des Louanges where 14 fathers of the Augustins-dechausses sang Jacob's praises in relays of two, day and night, to music she herself composed. But annoyed that they sang out of tune, she evicted them after five years and replaced them with the apparently more musical Order of the Petits-Augustins. The archaeologist Alexandre Lenoir later converted the space into the Musee des Monuments Francais, which saved the chapel from Revolutionary destruction.
beats.source_passage: The Beaux-Arts school ahead, at 14 rue Bonaparte, occupies part of the convent built by Marguerite de Valois in 1608

beats.script_body: Across the street from the Institut de France once stood Queen Margot's early 17th-century palace, its entrance at the present number 6 rue de Seine. Married against her will at 19 to her coarse provincial cousin Henri of Navarre, Margot led a scandalous love life that began when she was 11. Her brother Henri III publicly recited the list of her lovers at a ball in the Louvre. Banished for 18 years by Henri IV, she agreed to annul their marriage so long as she could keep the title of Queen. When she returned to Paris in 1605, aged 52, she built her palace along the Seine on land bought from the University, opposite her beloved Louvre.
physical_cues: n 6 rue de Seine where palace entrance was
beats.source_passage: Across the street from the Institut de France was situated Queen Margot's early 17th-century palace

opening_hours_basis: A fine arts school behind gates with restricted access; gated, hours not confidently known; left unfiltered.
visit_basis: Fine arts school with a courtyard gate and historic facades on rue Bonaparte; walk-by only, time to look through the gates at the former convent buildings.
judgement_basis: A gated art school with courtyards closed to the public, offering no free public seating and no open, populated space at night on its quiet side street.
queue_basis: Walked by only; the art school's courtyard and street facade are viewed without any ticketed entry or line.

name: Les Deux Magots
short_description: Iconic literary cafe on Place Saint-Germain-des-Pres, symbol of post-war Parisian intellectual life.

beats.script_body: The terrace of the Deux Magots on Place Saint-Germain-des-Pres, overflowing with people in fine weather, is the gateway to the post-war era that put Saint-Germain on the map. Nearby on Boulevard Saint-Germain, the celebrated Flore was the haunt of Jean-Paul Sartre and Simone de Beauvoir during the dark years of the Occupation. Across the street, the Drugstore Publicis replaced the Royal Saint-Germain. And on the same pavement, the Brasserie Lipp's setting has remained unchanged — a constellation of legendary establishments that defined Left Bank intellectual life.
physical_cues: terrace of Deux Magots on Place Saint-Germain-des-Pres
Cafe de Flore on Boulevard Saint-Germain
beats.source_passage: the terrace of the Deux Magots, overflowing with people in fine weather

opening_hours_basis: Listed as walk-by-only, an iconic cafe experienced from the square rather than entered on this tour, treated as not gated.
visit_basis: Famous cafe terrace on the square; walk-by only, a few minutes to take in the frontage and terrace from the pavement.
judgement_basis: A café on a busy boulevard corner where children have no enclosed space and its only seating is a paid terrace, but the square and boulevard around it are brightly lit and busy well into the night.
queue_basis: Walked by only and in any case a café with no security or ticketed entry; there is no queue to price for a tour stop.

name: Hotel d'York
short_description: Former hotel at 56 rue Jacob where the peace treaty between England and the United States was signed on 3 September 1783.

beats.script_body: At number 56 rue Jacob stood the Hotel d'York, where on 3 September 1783 at 9 am, the peace treaty between England and the United States of America was signed by the English representative David Hartley and his American counterparts Benjamin Franklin, John Jay and John Adams. Adams returned with his family the following September while looking for a permanent home, eventually settling in Auteuil. Nearby at number 52, Benjamin Franklin had already stayed at the Hotel de Hambourg in 1777, while waiting for permanent lodging before moving to Passy.
beats.source_passage: N 56 at the time was the Hotel d'York, where the peace treaty between England and the United States of America was signed at 9 am, on 3 September 1783

opening_hours_basis: A former hotel building noted for its historic facade viewed from the pavement, not gated.
visit_basis: Facade of the building where the 1783 peace treaty was signed; a few minutes to read the plaque and take in the street, nothing to enter as a visit.
judgement_basis: A former hotel building on the narrow, quiet rue Jacob offering no enclosed play space, no public seating, and a deserted, dim street after dark.
queue_basis: A historic building marked by a plaque and seen from the street; there is no interior visit and no queue.

name: Natalie Barney Salon
short_description: Former home of Natalie Barney at 20 rue Jacob, where she hosted her legendary literary salon for 60 years, featuring the Temple de l'Amitie.

beats.script_body: Behind the fence at number 20 rue Jacob was the 'sanctuary' of Natalie Barney, the glamorous Amazon who rode in the Bois de Boulogne wearing a bowler hat and black bow tie. For 60 years, French and American literati gathered in this shady courtyard with its creeping ivy. A mock Greek temple, Le Temple de l'Amitie, provided hedonistic atmosphere and shelter from the cold. When Barney arrived in 1909, tea and cake were the rule, but when the expatriates turned up in the 1920s, she reluctantly switched to champagne and whisky. Paul Valery read his works here but dropped her once elected an Academicien. Georges Antheil rehearsed his scandalous Ballet mecanique in the temple.
physical_cues: courtyard visible through fence at n 20
beats.source_passage: the 'sanctuary' of Natalie Barney, the glamorous Amazon

opening_hours_basis: A former private home viewed as a facade from the street, walk-by-only; not gated.
visit_basis: Private house frontage at 20 rue Jacob; walk-by only, a few minutes to read the story and glimpse the courtyard, the Temple de l'Amitie is not publicly accessible.
judgement_basis: A private former residence on the narrow rue Jacob with no public interior access, no seating, and a quiet, unlit residential street that empties after dark.
queue_basis: A private former residence seen only from the street with no public interior; there is nothing to queue for.

name: Hotel d'Angleterre Paris
short_description: Historic hotel at 44 rue Jacob where Washington Irving stayed in 1805, and where Hemingway and Hadley first lodged in Paris in December 1921.

beats.script_body: At number 44 rue Jacob, the Hotel d'Angleterre welcomed many literary visitors over the centuries. Sherwood Anderson recommended it to the newly-wed Hemingways when they arrived in Paris in December 1921. Anderson himself had reportedly paid 75 cents per night for a double room. The lovely 18th-century building now has a patio for breakfast on fine days.
beats.source_passage: Sherwood Anderson paid 75 cents per night for a double room, and therefore recommended it to the newly-wed Hemingways

opening_hours_basis: A working hotel seen from the street as a facade, walk-by-only; not gated.
visit_basis: Working hotel facade on a quiet street where Hemingway first lodged; walk-by only, a couple of minutes to read the plaque.
judgement_basis: A private hotel frontage on the narrow, quiet rue Jacob with no traffic-free running space, no free seating, and a residential street with little foot traffic or lighting at night.
queue_basis: A working hotel viewed from the street with no public ticketed entry and no line to stand in.

name: Rue de Buci Market
short_description: The most exciting and colourful market in the 6th arrondissement, a bustling spot since the time of Henri IV.

beats.script_body: On 2 September 1792, this bustling junction served as a recruiting ground for volunteers for 'the defence of the motherland' — in reality, for the three-day slaughter of the September Massacres. The first four victims, new detainees on their way to the abbey prison, were slain at this very street junction by the delirious mob. In 1848, a barricade was erected here on the first day of that year's Revolution, to the fervent cries of 'Vive la Republique!' Today this is a place of peace and fun, especially when the jazz musicians are about.
physical_cues: junction of rue de Buci and rue de Seine
beats.source_passage: On 2 September 1792 it was a fine recruiting-ground for volunteers for the defence of the motherland

opening_hours_basis: An open-air street market along the pavement with no gate or door between street and stalls, not gated.
visit_basis: Bustling open street market of stalls and cafe-lined blocks to walk slowly and browse; the whole experience is outdoors along the street, nothing to enter.
judgement_basis: A bustling market street with pedestrian and vehicle traffic, dense stalls and crowds where a child cannot run free and there is no quiet free seating, but it is lit and populated into the evening.
queue_basis: An open-air street market you stroll through; there is no gate, ticket, or security, so no line to enter.
